name: Duodenum
func: The first part of the small intestine, a C-shaped tube that receives food from the stomach plus bile and pancreatic juice. Here acid is neutralised and most chemical digestion begins.

levels.kid:
The **duodenum** is the very first part of your **small intestine**. It's shaped like the letter C and it curls around a soft organ called the pancreas, right after your stomach.

When the soupy food leaves your stomach, it's full of acid. The duodenum is the mixing station! Two helpers squirt juices into it through a tiny opening: **bile** from your liver and gallbladder, which breaks fat into tiny drops like dish soap does, and **pancreatic juice**, which is full of enzymes that chop up sugars, proteins and fats.

The pancreatic juice also neutralises the acid, so the food isn't sour any more and the intestine doesn't get hurt.

The duodenum is only about as long as a ruler and a half, but a lot of work happens there!
levels.hs:
The **duodenum** is about **25 cm long** and is the shortest, widest and most fixed part of the small intestine. It curves in a **C shape** around the **head of the pancreas**, at about the level of **L1–L3**. Most of it is **retroperitoneal** (behind the peritoneum, stuck to the back wall), except its first few centimetres.

It has **four parts**:
1. **Superior (1st)**: starts at the **pylorus** at L1. Its first 2–3 cm, the **duodenal bulb (ampulla)**, is mobile and is the commonest site of **duodenal ulcers**. The **gastroduodenal artery**, common bile duct and portal vein lie behind it.
2. **Descending (2nd)**: runs down beside the head of the pancreas, in front of the right kidney. Here the **major duodenal papilla** opens, where the **common bile duct** and **main pancreatic duct** empty, usually joined in the **hepatopancreatic ampulla (of Vater)**, controlled by the **sphincter of Oddi**.
3. **Horizontal (3rd)**: crosses from right to left at L3, passing between the **aorta** behind and the **superior mesenteric artery and vein** in front.
4. **Ascending (4th)**: rises to the **duodenojejunal flexure**, held up by the **suspensory ligament (of Treitz)**, where it continues as the **jejunum**.

The duodenum neutralises stomach acid, mixes chyme with bile and pancreatic enzymes, and absorbs **iron** and calcium.
levels.college:
**Histology**: the duodenum has the small intestine's features (**circular folds** or plicae circulares, **villi**, **crypts of Lieberkühn**) plus a unique feature: **Brunner's glands** in the submucosa, which secrete alkaline mucus to protect against acid.

A **minor duodenal papilla**, about 2 cm above the major one, drains the **accessory pancreatic duct** (of Santorini).

**Blood supply** sits at an embryological boundary: the duodenum lies at the junction of the **foregut** and **midgut**, roughly at the major papilla. Above that, it's supplied by the **superior pancreaticoduodenal arteries** (from the gastroduodenal artery, coeliac trunk); below it, by the **inferior pancreaticoduodenal arteries** (from the **superior mesenteric artery**). The two arcades anastomose around the pancreatic head, so the duodenum and pancreatic head share blood supply, which is why surgeons usually remove them together.

**Hormones from the duodenum** (from enteroendocrine cells):
- **Secretin** (S cells): released when acid enters; makes the pancreas and bile ducts secrete **bicarbonate**-rich fluid.
- **Cholecystokinin (CCK)** (I cells): released by fats and proteins; makes the **gallbladder contract**, relaxes the sphincter of Oddi and stimulates pancreatic **enzyme** secretion.
- **GIP** (K cells): increases insulin release after eating (an **incretin**).
- **Motilin**: drives the migrating motor complex between meals.

These hormones also slow **gastric emptying**, matching the rate of food delivery to how fast the duodenum can process it.

**Enteropeptidase (enterokinase)**, an enzyme on the duodenal brush border, activates **trypsinogen** to **trypsin**, which then activates the other pancreatic enzymes.
levels.phd:
**Iron absorption** is concentrated in the duodenum. Dietary non-haem iron (Fe³⁺) is reduced to Fe²⁺ by **duodenal cytochrome b (DcytB)** and enters enterocytes through **DMT1**, a proton-coupled transporter, helped by the acidic chyme arriving from the stomach. Iron leaves through **ferroportin** on the basolateral membrane, oxidised by **hephaestin**, and binds transferrin. The liver hormone **hepcidin** controls the whole system by causing ferroportin to be internalised and degraded; this is why inflammation (which raises hepcidin) causes anaemia, and why loss of hepcidin causes iron overload in **hereditary haemochromatosis**.

**Nutrient sensing**: duodenal enteroendocrine cells express taste-like receptors, fatty acid receptors (**FFAR1/GPR40, GPR120**) and amino acid sensors. Some, called **neuropods**, form synapses with vagal sensory neurons, relaying nutrient information to the brain in milliseconds via glutamate, a recent finding that changed views of gut–brain communication.

**Incretin effect**: oral glucose triggers far more insulin release than the same glucose given intravenously, due to **GIP** (duodenum) and **GLP-1** (more distal L cells). Drugs mimicking GLP-1 are now major treatments for type 2 diabetes and obesity.

**Coeliac disease**: in genetically susceptible people (HLA-**DQ2/DQ8**), gluten peptides (gliadin), modified by **tissue transglutaminase**, are presented to T cells, causing an immune attack on the duodenal and jejunal lining: **villous atrophy**, **crypt hyperplasia** and more intraepithelial lymphocytes (graded by the **Marsh classification**). Antibodies to tissue transglutaminase are the main blood test.

**Duodenal–biliary interface**: the sphincter of Oddi is regulated by CCK and nitric oxide, coordinating bile flow with meals. Duodenal-mucosal resurfacing, which ablates the lining endoscopically, is being researched as a metabolic therapy.
levels.expert:
**Duodenal ulcer**: the classic patient has epigastric pain that's **better with eating** and wakes them at night (versus gastric ulcers, often worse with food). Causes: **H. pylori** (most), **NSAIDs**, and rarely **Zollinger–Ellison syndrome**, a gastrin-secreting tumour producing many ulcers, including in unusual places beyond the bulb. A **posterior** bulb ulcer may erode the **gastroduodenal artery**, causing major bleeding; an **anterior** one tends to **perforate**, releasing air under the diaphragm.

**Endoscopy**: the papilla is reached with a side-viewing duodenoscope for **ERCP** (endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography), used to remove bile duct stones and place stents. Post-ERCP pancreatitis is its commonest complication.

**Obstruction**:
- **Duodenal atresia** in newborns: bilious vomiting with the "**double bubble**" sign on X-ray (gas in stomach and duodenal bulb), associated with Down syndrome.
- **Annular pancreas**: a ring of pancreas around the 2nd part.
- **Superior mesenteric artery syndrome**: after rapid weight loss, the angle between the SMA and aorta narrows and squeezes the 3rd part, causing vomiting after meals.
- **Malrotation with volvulus** in infants: a surgical emergency, with bilious vomiting; contrast studies show the duodenojejunal flexure in the wrong place.

**Trauma**: retroperitoneal duodenal injury (e.g. handlebar injury in children) can be missed; CT shows retroperitoneal air or fluid.

**Cancer near the papilla** (ampullary, distal bile duct or pancreatic head) causes **painless jaundice**. The operation is the **Whipple procedure** (pancreaticoduodenectomy), which removes the duodenum, pancreatic head, distal bile duct and gallbladder together, because of their shared blood supply.

**Neuro aside**: copper is absorbed mainly in the stomach and duodenum, so after operations that bypass them (like gastric bypass), **copper deficiency** can cause a spinal cord disorder (**myelopathy**) that looks just like B12 deficiency.

keyPoints: C-shaped, about 25 cm, wraps around the pancreatic head
Four parts; bile and pancreatic juice enter at the major papilla (2nd part)
Mostly retroperitoneal; ends at the ligament of Treitz
Secretin → bicarbonate; CCK → gallbladder contraction and enzymes

test.q: In which part of the duodenum do bile and pancreatic juice enter?
test.explain: The major duodenal papilla opens into the 2nd part.

test.q: The hormone that makes the gallbladder contract is ______.
test.explain: CCK is released by I cells in response to fat and protein.

test.q: The 3rd part of the duodenum passes between which two vessels?
test.explain: It crosses between the aorta behind and the SMA in front, where it can be compressed (SMA syndrome).

test.q: Submucosal glands unique to the duodenum are called ______ glands.
test.explain: Brunner's glands secrete alkaline mucus that protects against stomach acid.

test.q: A newborn's X-ray shows a 'double bubble'. Likely diagnosis?
test.explain: Gas trapped in the stomach and duodenal bulb forms two bubbles when the duodenum is blocked.
